trivia: Zinedine Zidane, who won France the 1998 World Cup with two headers in the final, is the son of immigrants from my mountainous Kabylie region.
reveal: Zinedine Zidane, whose parents came from Kabylie

trivia: Over the last 50 years my most popular boys' names have been Mohamed, Ahmed, Abdelkader, Ali and Youcef. For girls, Meriem, Fatima and Amina keep coming back, although girls' names follow fashions much more than boys' do.

Many of my families have had surnames for less than 150 years. A colonial law of 1882 forced everyone to register a family name, and clerks sometimes handed out odd or mocking ones that families still carry.
Raï, the rebellious pop music born in the bars of a western port city, went global in 1992 when Cheb Khaled's song 'Didi' became a hit across Europe, the Middle East and India.
reveal: Raï from Oran, and Cheb Khaled's 'Didi'

trivia: Among my desert Tuareg, the imzad is a one-stringed fiddle played only by women. Its music was believed to heal the sick and to spur warriors on, and UNESCO protected it in 2013.

In my deep south, it's the men who veil their faces, not the women. Tuareg men wind an indigo cloth around the head that can be several metres long, and the dye stains their skin blue, which earned them the nickname 'blue men of the desert'.
reveal: The tagelmust of the Tuareg men

trivia: Yves Saint Laurent, the designer who put women in tuxedos, was born and grew up in Oran, a city on my Mediterranean coast.
reveal: Yves Saint Laurent, born in Oran in 1936

trivia: My capital's signature outfit for brides is the karakou, a fitted velvet jacket heavily embroidered with gold thread.
In my northern mountains, women's dresses blaze with colour: bright yellow, red and green bands and zigzag ribbons, worn with a striped wool sash and heavy silver jewellery set with red coral.
Since 2016 the Berber language, Tamazight, has been official here alongside Arabic. It has its own ancient alphabet, Tifinagh, which you can now see on government buildings and signs.
My name in Arabic means 'the islands'. It comes from my capital, which was named after a few small islands off its harbour that were later joined to the mainland to make the port.

French is spoken across my cities and printed in many newspapers, making me one of the largest French-speaking countries in the world. Yet French has no official status here, and I've never joined the international organisation of French-speaking countries.
reveal: French in Algeria; Algeria is not a member of the Francophonie (OIF)

trivia: On 12 January my people celebrate Yennayer, the Amazigh (Berber) New Year, with couscous and big family meals. In 2018 it became a national public holiday for the first time.

On 5 July 1962, my independence day, crowds poured into the streets after more than 130 years of colonial rule. The date was chosen on purpose: it was 132 years to the day since the invaders had captured my capital.
reveal: 5 July 1962, 132 years after France took Algiers on 5 July 1830

trivia: In a remote Saharan oasis town, Tuareg men and women perform the Sbeiba every year, a ritual dance-duel of drummers and swordsmen that re-enacts an ancient truce between two rival villages. UNESCO listed it in 2014.
Couscous is so central to my kitchens that in 2020 I joined my neighbours Morocco, Tunisia and Mauritania in a rare joint bid, and UNESCO listed it as shared heritage.

My favourite street snack is a slab of baked chickpea-flour flan stuffed into a baguette with cumin and harissa. Its name comes from the Spanish word for 'hot', because Spanish soldiers are said to have invented it while besieged in a western port city, and TasteAtlas has crowned it the world's best street food.

My most prized date, Deglet Nour, means 'date of light' because a ripe one is so translucent you can almost see the stone inside against the sun. TasteAtlas ranks it the second-best date in the world.
reveal: Deglet Nour dates from Biskra and Ouargla

trivia: At the 1982 World Cup my team stunned West Germany 2-1. Then West Germany and Austria played out a suspiciously gentle 1-0 that knocked us out. The scandal was so big that FIFA has made the final group games kick off at the same time ever since.
reveal: The 'Disgrace of Gijón', West Germany 1-0 Austria, 1982

trivia: In April 1958, two months before the World Cup, some of the best footballers in France secretly slipped out of the country, two of them stars expected to play for France. They reappeared in Tunis as a rebel national team for my independence movement.
reveal: The FLN football team, with Rachid Mekhloufi and Mustapha Zitouni

trivia: In 1992 Hassiba Boulmerka won my first-ever Olympic gold, in the 1,500 metres. Back home some preachers condemned her for running in shorts, and she trained under threat for the rest of her career.
My national animal is the fennec, a tiny desert fox with enormous ears that shed heat. My national football team is nicknamed 'Les Fennecs' after it.

On a remote Saharan plateau stand just 233 wild cypress trees, survivors from a time when the desert was green. Radiocarbon dating puts the oldest at more than 1,700 years old, and almost no young trees are growing to replace them.
reveal: The Saharan cypress (tarout) of Tassili n'Ajjer

trivia: In my coastal mountain forests live Barbary macaques, the only monkeys in Africa north of the Sahara. The famous apes of Gibraltar are the same species and descend from North African populations.
Since Sudan split in two in 2011, I've been the largest country in Africa, and more than four-fifths of me is Sahara desert.
A desert town I call the 'gateway to the Sahara' has woken up to snow on its orange dunes several times since 2016. In 2018 up to 40 cm fell just outside town, before melting away by the afternoon.
reveal: Ain Sefra, the 'gateway to the desert'

trivia: High on a sandstone plateau in my Sahara are more than 15,000 rock paintings and engravings showing giraffes, hippos, cattle herds and swimmers, a record of when this desert was green.
The Casbah of Algiers, a steep maze of whitewashed Ottoman houses and alleys above the harbour, was the setting of the famous 1966 film The Battle of Algiers and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Five fortified desert towns of sand-coloured cube houses, each built around a mosque on a hilltop, so impressed the architect Le Corbusier that he sketched them on visits in 1931 and 1933 and drew on them in his own work.
In my eastern highlands lies a Roman city founded by Emperor Trajan around 100 AD for retired soldiers. It's laid out on such a perfect grid of streets that it's nicknamed the 'Pompeii of Africa'.
One of my oldest cities sits on a rock cut off by a gorge up to 200 metres deep, so it's stitched together by a series of dizzying bridges and nicknamed the 'City of Bridges'.
I'm called the 'land of a million and a half martyrs' after my war of independence from France, fought from 1954 to 1962, which ended 132 years of colonial rule.
Saint Augustine, one of Christianity's most influential thinkers, was born in my land in 354 AD and spent most of his life here as bishop of the ancient port of Hippo.
reveal: Saint Augustine, born in Thagaste (Souk Ahras), bishop of Hippo (Annaba)

trivia: On 13 February 1960, in the middle of my independence war, France exploded its first atomic bomb in my Sahara, about four times as powerful as the Hiroshima bomb. Code-named 'Blue Jerboa' after a desert rodent, it was the first of 17 French nuclear tests on my soil.

In 2018 archaeologists digging in my northern highlands found stone tools and butchered animal bones about 2.4 million years old. That's almost as old as anything from East Africa, and it challenges the idea that East Africa alone was the cradle of toolmaking.
Pipelines run under the Mediterranean from my desert gas fields straight to Spain and to Italy via Tunisia. In 2025 I supplied about 13-14% of the EU's gas imports, and roughly a third of Italy's.
reveal: The Transmed (to Italy) and Medgaz (to Spain) pipelines

trivia: I'm among the world's top three or four date growers and grow more than 100 varieties. In 2024 I exported nearly 67,000 tonnes of dates, many of them the prized Deglet Nour.
In 1964 my coast became home to the world's first large commercial liquefied-natural-gas plant, chilling gas into a liquid so tankers could ship it across the sea to Britain.
reveal: The CAMEL LNG plant at Arzew, which shipped to Britain's Canvey Island

trivia: Visitors to my Sahara almost always take home a 'desert rose', a cluster of gypsum crystals that grows under the sand into the shape of rose petals.
reveal: The Saharan desert rose (rose des sables)

trivia: In my northern mountains, jewellers make chunky silver pieces glowing with blue, green and yellow enamel and set with red coral. The craft dates back to the 15th century and is a favourite souvenir.
reveal: Kabyle silver jewellery from Beni Yenni

trivia: Desert travellers here buy hand-engraved silver 'crosses' from Tuareg silversmiths. Each oasis and region has its own design.
